readerTitle: Six promises on a van, and nobody remembers one
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Volvo와 '안전') + 가상 사례 (배관 업체, 청소 업체, 지역 화물 운송사)
insight: 고객은 한 회사에 대해 한 가지만 기억한다. 그러니 무엇을 기억하게 할지 직접 고르고, 나머지는 포기해야 한다.
misconception: 강점을 많이 내세울수록 더 많은 고객을 끌어온다. 'quality'처럼 모든 것을 담는 단어 하나면 충분하다.

sources.text: Ries, A. & Trout, J. (1993). The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing. 'The Law of Focus' 장
Volvo Cars, company history: the three-point seat belt (Nils Bohlin, 1959)

factChecks.note: Ries & Trout(1993)의 'Law of Focus'가 '고객의 머릿속에서 한 단어를 소유하라'는 내용인지 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 직접 인용 없이 요지만 적었습니다.
Volvo 엔지니어 Nils Bohlin이 1959년 3점식 안전벨트를 개발했고, Volvo가 특허를 다른 제조사에 무료로 개방했다는 내용을 Volvo 공식 자료로 다시 확인하세요.
'많은 운전자가 안전한 차와 Volvo를 거의 같은 뜻으로 여기게 됐다'는 문장은 정성적 서술입니다. 설문 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 필요하면 브랜드 인식 조사 출처를 찾아 보완하세요.

cards.title: Six promises on a van, and nobody remembers one
body: Two plumbing vans park on the same street. The first lists six promises: fast, reliable, affordable, friendly, licensed, 24/7. The second says one thing: *On time, or the visit is free.*
A month later, a neighbor's pipe bursts. She remembers the second van. She can't recall a single word from the first.

image.label: Two vans: one covered in slogans, one with a single line
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 주택가에 배관 업체 밴 두 대. 왼쪽 밴은 문구 여섯 개로 빽빽하고 흐릿하게, 오른쪽 밴은 큰 글씨로 "On time, or it's free" 한 줄만. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: One line for your flyers.
body: You run a house-cleaning company. Your team is careful, quick, uses eco-friendly products, charges fair prices and is friendly.
You're printing new flyers and van signs with room for one main line. What goes on it?

options.text: All five strengths, so every customer finds a reason
options.feedback: It covers every base, but five claims compete for one glance, and rivals print the same five. Nothing sticks.

options.text: One word you can prove, like "spotless", backed by a free re-clean
options.feedback: You stop talking about price and speed. In return, customers get one clear reason to pick you and one word to remember you by.
One word is the right instinct. But every cleaner claims quality, so it can never belong to you.

cards.title: Why the long list loses.
body: A customer gives your flyer a few seconds. In that time, a list doesn't land as five reasons. It lands as noise.
Your rivals also print the same list. When everyone is fast, friendly and affordable, those words stop telling businesses apart.
The van with one promise isn't saying less. It's the only one saying something a customer can repeat to a friend.

cards.title: Owning one word
body: **Owning a word** means that when customers think of one quality in your market, your name comes to mind first.

Marketing strategists Al Ries and Jack Trout argued for this in *The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing* (1993). Their view: the strongest position is one simple word that you hold in the customer's mind and rivals don't.
It's narrower than a list of strengths. That's the point.

image.label: A head with one word glowing inside, other words fading out
image.brief: 사람 머리 실루엣 안에 단어 하나("Spotless")만 밝게 빛나고, 주변에 "Fast", "Cheap", "Friendly", "Eco" 같은 단어들이 흐려지며 밖으로 흩어지는 인포그래픽.

cards.title: Volvo and "safety"
body: In 1959, Volvo engineer Nils Bohlin developed the three-point seat belt, the over-the-shoulder design most cars use today. Volvo let other carmakers use the patent for free.
For decades after, Volvo kept **safety** at the center of its cars and its advertising. Many drivers came to treat "safe car" and "Volvo" as nearly the same idea.
Other carmakers built safe cars too. But the word was already taken.

image.label: A car silhouette wrapped in a seat belt shape
image.brief: 단순한 승용차 실루엣을 3점식 안전벨트 모양의 띠가 감싸는 일러스트. 옆에 "1959"와 "Safety" 텍스트. 실제 Volvo 로고, 엠블럼, 차량 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The word can be small.
body: It doesn't have to be a grand quality. Often it's one customer type or one job:
list: **A bakery:** "sourdough", not "fresh bread, pastries and coffee"
cards.callout: Small and yours beats big and shared.
cards.softwareNote: Many software tools pitch themselves as "all-in-one". A product that owns one word, like "simple" or "for freelancers", is easier to recommend, because users can explain it to a friend in one sentence.

cards.title: Owning a word has a price.
body: You give up the other words. A cleaner known for "spotless" will lose some customers hunting for the cheapest quote. That's the cost.
The word must be true every time. One sloppy job hurts a "spotless" brand more than an ordinary one.
And don't chase a word a rival already owns. Fighting a leader for its own word is expensive and rarely works. Look for an open one.

cards.title: Now it's a freight company.
body: You run a regional trucking firm. The big national carrier is known for reach: it goes everywhere. Your drivers are unusually careful, and your damage claims are low.
Which word do you build around?

options.text: "Everywhere": add routes and say you cover the country too
options.feedback: You'd be fighting the leader for its own word, with fewer trucks and a smaller budget.

options.text: "Careful": handling for fragile freight like glass, electronics and medical gear
options.feedback: You give up shippers who only want the widest map. You gain a word the leader doesn't own, and a reason to charge more.

options.text: "Cheapest": undercut the national carrier on price
options.feedback: Price is a word you can own, but any rival can take it back with one price cut, and it squeezes your margins.

cards.title: Pick one word, and give up the rest.
body: Customers remember one thing about a business, if that. Choose which thing, make it true every day, and stop diluting it.
**Try it today:** ask three customers to describe your business in one word. If the answers differ, you don't own a word yet.
